name: Bianca Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, Bianca, and thank you for seeing me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hartley's, it's the family-owned supermarket on Church Street, been there forty years. I'm on the till most of the day, and I do the newspapers and the lottery at the kiosk end. Mr Hartley's son runs it now, and he still knows half the customers by name.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's local and people trust us, you see the same faces at Sunday Mass and then on Monday at the till. I'm still learning the stock system, the scanner gun confuses me and I've ordered the wrong milk twice. The hard part is the money, I'm on the lowest rate, and since the discount chain opened by the bypass we've lost a lot of the weekly shop.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Marco, he's a mechanic at the bus depot. We're getting married next June at Saint Anne's, and we're saving for that, slowly. I don't use any AI things, I don't trust them, and my phone is for calls and the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's mostly talk. I always thought so, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad says, that people get excited about gadgets and then go back to normal. At the till I'd tell customers not to believe everything they read. I don't post online, except pictures in the family chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changing isn't good either when the family shop I work in is losing out to the discount chain. Mr Hartley already cut Sunday afternoon opening. If he cuts more hours, I've got less than a month of money and a wedding to pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard and ask Mr Hartley for more shifts on the kiosk side, because the lottery still brings people in. Marco and I would cut the wedding guest list a bit and maybe do the reception in the church hall instead of the hotel. I'd also ask my aunt about extra cleaning work at her office on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's an old worry. It's not about computers, it's about whether Hartley's lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Hartley if he cut more hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I understand, because I do, it's his family's business and he's trying. But I'd ask him to give me notice so I can find something else. I wouldn't want to make him feel worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about the discount chain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They can sell cheap because they don't care about the town. People choose them, that's their right, but then they complain when the high street closes. I'd rather pay a bit more and keep Hartley's.

say: People get excited about **gadgets** and then go back to normal.
I'd tell customers at the till not to **believe everything** they read.
think: **Hartley's** is struggling against the discount chain on the bypass.
More **hour cuts** would hit with under a month saved and a **wedding** coming.
do: Ask for more **kiosk shifts** on lottery and newspapers.
Move the **wedding reception** to the church hall.
Ask her aunt for **Saturday cleaning** work.
feel: **Worried**, but it's an **old worry** about whether Hartley's lasts.
S0.quote: Nothing changing isn't good either when the family shop I work in is losing out to the discount chain.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **family-run shop's survival**, not AI.
Loyal to her employer and would ask only for **notice**.
Blames customers' choices and the **discount chain**, while respecting their right to choose.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hartley for more kiosk shifts
Hold the wedding reception in the church hall
Take Saturday cleaning work at her aunt's office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking jobs, writing and booking and so on. That doesn't sound like Hartley's, we still do the ordering on a clipboard half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it doesn't affect people like us much, we're on our feet all day. At church people would talk about their kids in offices. I'd say pray for them, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But I think the big chains would use it to get even cheaper, with their computers doing all the ordering and pricing. That makes it harder for Hartley's. The AI isn't coming for my till, it's helping the big chain beat the family shop I work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work. I'd ask Marco if the bus depot has any jobs, like in the canteen or cleaning, because the depot feels safer. And we'd put a bit more aside every month for the wedding and less on going out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit sad. Like watching the town slowly lose things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any of the new tools if Hartley's brought them in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Hartley asked, I'd try, because he's been good to me. But I'd be slow, and I'd need someone to sit with me. I'd never use them at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if it got hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, my parents and Marco's mother. Then the parish, there's always someone who knows of a job. I'd go to them before any government office.

say: People on their **feet all day** aren't affected much.
I'd say at church to **pray** for the office workers.
think: The big **chains** would use AI to get even **cheaper**.
The AI isn't coming for my till; it's helping the **chain beat us**.
do: Keep her **head down** and keep working.
Ask Marco about **canteen or cleaning** jobs at the bus depot.
Put more aside for the **wedding** and less on going out.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit **sad** about the town losing things.
S1.quote: The AI isn't coming for my till, it's helping the big chain beat the family shop I work in.
fieldNote: Sees AI as a weapon for **big chains** against her independent employer.
Would try new tools only out of **loyalty** to her boss.
Turns to **family and parish** before any government help.

steps.text: Keep working the till and kiosk as normal
Ask about canteen or cleaning jobs at the bus depot
Lean on her parents and parish contacts for job leads
Put more aside for the wedding each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? And robots by 2031? I don't believe it, but if it's true, that's terrible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's against nature, people need work to have dignity. At church we'd talk about it after Mass. I'd say the companies that do this should be ashamed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Hartley's closes, because the chains will have robots and AI and be so cheap no one can compete. Then my till job is gone, maybe before the robots even come. I'm twenty-seven, I've only ever worked tills, and I don't know anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Marco about putting the wedding off, which breaks my heart, or making it very small. I'd ask my parents if we could live with them for a while. I'd go to the parish priest and ask if anyone needs help, cleaning, care for older people, anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I can't see where we'd land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marco about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's still get married, but at the registry office with just family, and do the big church one later. He'd say no, his mother wants the church. We'd probably argue and then pray about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Hartley's might close before the robots come. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the chains' computers would do their buying and pricing straight away. They'd drop prices and we'd lose customers in the first year. Mr Hartley can't afford to lose money for long.

say: Work gives people **dignity**; this is against nature.
Companies that do this should be **ashamed**.
We'd talk it over after **Mass** at church.
think: **Hartley's closes** before the robots even come, beaten on price.
I've only ever worked **tills** and know nothing else.
do: Make the **wedding small** or put it off.
Move in with her **parents** for a while.
Ask the **parish priest** about cleaning or care work.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven, I've only ever worked tills, and I don't know anything else.
fieldNote: Expects her **employer to close** within a year as chains cut prices with AI.
The **wedding** is the first casualty and a source of family tension.
No plan beyond **family and parish**; no savings to make one.

steps.text: Shrink the wedding to a registry office ceremony
Move in with her parents to save rent
Ask the parish priest about cleaning or care jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. Still fast, but maybe we'd have time to marry properly first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that work matters and companies should think of families. But I'd say it with less panic. At the till I'd tell customers to keep shopping local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Hartley's would last a few more years, maybe till 2031 or so, then struggle. That gives me time to get married and find something steadier. Care work keeps coming back to me, because old people need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next June as planned, but small, then start looking at care jobs in the following year. My aunt works in a care home and she says they always need people. I'd keep Hartley's as long as it lasts and do care training on my days off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe in this one. There's room for the wedding, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for care training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the care home pays for the basic certificate if you work there. So I'd do weekend shifts there first. It's hard work, but it's honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay at Hartley's longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If people in town kept shopping there. That's why I'd tell everyone at church to buy their bread there and not at the chain. It sounds small but it's what we can do.

say: **Work matters** and companies should think of **families**.
I'd tell customers at the till to **keep shopping local**.
think: Hartley's might last until about **2031**, then struggle.
**Care work** keeps coming back to me because old people need a person.
do: Get married next June as planned, but **small**.
Do **weekend care home shifts** so the home pays for training.
Urge her church to buy bread at **Hartley's**.
S3.quote: Care work keeps coming back to me, because old people need a person.
fieldNote: Still expects her **till job to go**, but five years lets her marry first.
Plans to enter **care** through her aunt's care home.
Sees **shopping local** as the small thing her community can do.

steps.text: Marry next June in a small church service
Work weekend shifts at her aunt's care home
Get the basic care certificate paid by the home
Urge church friends to buy their bread at Hartley's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. That's a long way off. I'd be thirty-seven with children, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families to plan and the government shouldn't need to step in much. People should look after their own. I'd still tell everyone to shop local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be alright, because ten years is enough to have a family and change to care. But Hartley's might still close for other reasons, the chain was hurting it before any AI. So I'm not calm, I'm just less scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry next June and keep working at Hartley's. In a few years I'd start care training, slowly, maybe once the first child is at school. We'd try to save for a deposit on a small house near my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. A bit of the old worry about money and the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI tools, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if I had to for a job. I'd want my sister to show me, she's good with that. But I don't want my children growing up talking to a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to do for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and with people, like a nurse or a mechanic like Marco. Something that can't be done from a phone. And I'd want them close to home.

say: There's time for **families to plan** without much government help.
People should **look after their own**, and still shop local.
think: Ten years is enough to have a **family** and change to **care**.
**Hartley's** might still close for reasons that predate AI.
do: Marry next June and **keep working** at Hartley's.
Start **care training** once the first child is at school.
Save for a **house deposit** near her parents.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, with the **old worry** about money and the shop.
S4.quote: I don't want my children growing up talking to a machine.
fieldNote: Less scared with ten years, but the **shop's struggle** keeps her anxious.
Plans her life around **marriage and children** first.
Wants future children in **hands-on**, people-facing work close to home.

steps.text: Marry next June and keep working at Hartley's
Start care training once the first child is at school
Save for a house deposit near her parents

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Hartley's would close and our wedding and everything would fall apart at once. What would help is apprenticeships for people like me in care or trades, paid while you learn. And for people to keep shopping at local places.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When things go wrong, my church is where people find work and food and company. Whatever happens with machines, I'd want those places kept alive.

headlineQuote: When things go wrong, my church is where people find work and food and company.
portrait: Bianca is 27, on the **till and kiosk** at Hartley's, a family-owned supermarket on Church Street.
She's engaged to **Marco**, a bus mechanic, and saving slowly for a **June wedding**.
She never uses AI and sees it mainly as a weapon for **big chains** against her shop.
She leans on family and **parish**, and looks to **care work** as her way out.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Hartley's would close and her **wedding** plans would collapse.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** in care or trades, and people **shopping local**.
